query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In corrosion‐resistant steels, heat-treatment–induced local chemical ordering that promotes chromium segregation to the surface and grain boundaries enhances the formation of a stable, Cr‐rich passive oxide film, thereby reducing the effective corrosion rate in aggressive chemical-processing and nuclear-power environments.
generation.material_initial_state: Low‐alloy or stainless steels with a uniform (random) solid‐solution distribution of alloying elements (including ~10–20% Cr) in their as-cast or as-rolled state.
generation.intervention: A controlled heat-treatment (or thermo-mechanical processing) designed to enhance short-range chemical ordering and induce local Cr segregation compared to untreated (baseline) steel.
generation.conditions: Exposure to simulated service environments such as high-temperature, high-pressure water chemistry representative of pressurized water reactor (PWR) primary systems or chemical plants containing corrosive agents (e.g., moderate chloride concentrations); tests performed at controlled temperatures (e.g., 320°C) and pressures.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent, Cr-enriched passive oxide layer (e.g., Cr2O3) along grain boundaries and surfaces that acts as a diffusion barrier against corrosive species.
generation.mechanism: The heat-treatment promotes local short-range ordering so that Cr atoms preferentially accumulate at surfaces and defects. This Cr segregation drives the in-situ formation of a dense, protective Cr-oxide film that limits the ingress of aggressive species and thereby reduces electrochemical dissolution rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steels subjected to the targeted heat-treatment will exhibit lower corrosion current densities (e.g., via potentiodynamic polarization) and reduced weight loss compared to their untreated counterparts; microanalysis will reveal a more homogeneous and thicker Cr-rich passive film in treated samples.
generation.baseline: Untreated steels with randomly distributed Cr, which form less uniform and thinner oxide films, leading to higher corrosion rates under identical environmental conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold in steels having sufficient Cr content (typically >10%) and under service conditions where passivation is thermodynamically favorable (e.g., moderate pH and temperatures typical of PWR primary water or certain chemical-processing media) but may not extend to extremely aggressive environments where alloy element dissolution is dominated by non-passivating processes.
generation.uncertainty: The precise degree of short-range order (or Cr segregation) required to yield a meaningful reduction in corrosion rates and the quantitative changes in electrochemical performance remain to be established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of steel specimens with identical bulk compositions. Subject one group to a controlled heat-treatment designed to enhance local Cr ordering (intervention group) while leaving the other group untreated (baseline group). Expose both groups to a simulated corrosive environment such as a high-temperature PWR primary water loop (e.g., 320°C, 11.3 MPa, borated and lithiated water) for a fixed duration (e.g., 20–60 days). Post-exposure, perform surface analysis (e.g., XPS, SEM/EDS) to characterize the passive films and determine corrosion damage via weight loss measurements and electrochemical polarization tests.
measurements: Corrosion current density from potentiodynamic polarization curves
Weight loss of specimens after exposure
Passive film composition and thickness via XPS and SEM/EDS
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to assess film stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated steels do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in corrosion current density, weight loss, or improved passive film characteristics compared to the untreated baseline (or if treated specimens show increased corrosion rates), then the hypothesis that enhanced Cr segregation via local chemical ordering is responsible for improved corrosion resistance will be falsified.

Combined effect of interstitial-substitutional elements on dislocation dynamics in nitrogen-added austenitic stainless steels

Abstract: Combined addition of interstitial-substitutional elements has been acknowledged to contribute to the increase in the strengths of steels. For further improvements in mechanical properties, their atomic-scale interaction mechanisms with dislocations are required to be examined. In this study, both high-resolution transmission electron microscopy and atom-probe tomography were used to correlate interstitial-substitutional elements with dislocation characteristics in austenitic stainless steels. Three types of dislocation core structures are identified and associated with their strain fields as well as N and Cr atoms in the N-added steels. It is revealed that N atoms interact elastically with the dislocations, followed by the segregation of Cr atoms via the chemical interaction between N and Cr atoms. This insight significantly improves the understanding of the multiple alloying mechanism in metallic materials such as interstitial alloys and high-entropy alloys.

Corrosion and Thermal Stability of CrMnFeNi High Entropy Alloy in Molten FLiBe Salt

Abstract: AbstractThe corrosion behavior of the FCC Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5 high entropy alloy (HEA) after exposure to molten FLiBe salt at 700 °C for 1000 hours, has been investigated. Results show that the HEA lost a higher mass compared to the reference 316 H stainless steel due to the dissolution of Mn into the molten salt. The loss of Mn from the alloy appeared to discourage the dissolution of Cr in the molten fluoride salts which is widely recognized as the mechanism of corrosion degradation. Thermal exposure at 700 °C for 1000 hours also led to the precipitation of an additional BCC phase Cr67Fe13Mn18.5Ni1.5, which was confirmed by CALPHAD predictions.Subject terms: Structural materials, Metals and alloys

Conclusions: The corrosion resistance of Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5 high entropy alloy in molten salts was tested after exposure to molten FLiBe salt at 700 °C for 1000 hours. The alloy lost significant mass compared to reference 316 H stainless steel which was attributed to the dissolution of Mn into the salt.
